archetype.name: Game Manager (dink-and-dunk)
archetype.definition: A short-area distributor who lives on quick, low-air-yard throws and needs accuracy and clean pockets to work, because the vertical game isn't carrying him.

report.headline: The 2025 breakout has evaporated; accuracy and turnovers have him near league bottom.
report.take:
Daniel Jones arrived in Indianapolis and had the best year of his career in 2025: 8.08 yards per attempt (7th), +0.193 EPA per play (11th), a 68% completion rate. Every other season of his career sat in the low-middle of the league, with EPA per play ranked anywhere from 12th to 53rd and yards per attempt in the high 30s to mid-50s. This year he has fallen below even that baseline: -0.184 EPA per dropback (45th of 55), 5.62 yards per attempt (47th), a CPOE of -6.79, and a league-worst 13 interceptions. The question isn't whether he is slumping. It's whether 2025 was the outlier, and the career line says it probably was.

The root problem is ball placement. His bad-throw rate is 18.2%, up 6.5 points from last year and back to where it sat in 2019-2021, after four straight seasons near 11-13%. That's not a scheme quirk. When the ball is off target, everything downstream breaks. The deep game is dead: 12.2% completions on 41 throws of 20+ air yards, no touchdowns, three picks, -19.2 EPA. Throws of 10+ yards complete at 34.9% with eight interceptions. Losing Alec Pierce, his vertical receiver, after two games removed the one player built to win those throws, and Jones has gotten more conservative to compensate, with aggressiveness down 3.2 points from last year. The line hasn't helped either; the offense's hit rate allowed ranks 28th.

Two details soften the picture slightly. Intermediate throws actually grade positive (+0.063 EPA per play), and so do throws over the middle. The problem there is turnovers, not production: five intermediate interceptions and five more over the middle. His targets also split sharply. Josh Downs (+0.198 per target) and Keenan Allen (+0.103) are producing. Tyler Warren (-0.204 on a team-high 59 targets) and Jonathan Taylor as a receiver (-0.164) are sinks. The wins don't vindicate him either. He posted -9.7 passing EPA in the Washington win and -11.3 against Miami, games carried by a run game that ranks 9th in EPA.

The direction is the worst part. Over the last three games his CPOE is -14.8 and his EPA per dropback is -0.307, both well below a season line that was already bad. His interception rate over the last five is 5.3%. Sacks have dropped lately, but the misses have gotten wilder: a 38.1% bad-throw rate against Miami and 25% at Houston. Nothing in the dossier points to a fix arriving soon, and his two starting tackles are out for the next game.

strengths.title: Downs and Allen remain functional
strengths.body: When the ball goes to his two veteran-style separators, the offense works. Downs and Allen are the only high-volume targets with positive EPA, which makes sense for a passer whose game is timing and short-to-intermediate windows. It's sustainable as long as play-calling funnels volume their way instead of to Warren and Taylor.

strengths.title: Short-yardage keepers convert
strengths.body: His designed runs have been nearly automatic for what they are asked to do, with a 78.6% success rate and +0.477 EPA per play, even at 1.79 yards a carry. These are sneaks and short-yardage keepers rather than open-field running, so on 14 plays this is a useful tool, not a source of fantasy value.

strengths.title: Sacks held below league average
strengths.body: Behind a line that ranks 28th in hit rate allowed, his 7.1% sack rate sits below the 7.8% league average, and he has taken fewer sacks over the last three games. He is getting the ball out rather than eating it. The catch is that some of those throwaways-turned-attempts are the inaccurate ones.

concerns.title: Accuracy back to early-career levels
concerns.body: His bad-throw rate of 18.2% ranks 41st of 45 and is 6.5 points worse than 2025. It matches his 2019-2021 Giants seasons, not the cleaner 2022-2025 stretch. Because this tracks with a trait he has shown before, it looks like a real regression rather than noise, and the last three games (CPOE -14.8) are the worst of it.

concerns.title: Turnovers on every level
concerns.body: His 13 interceptions are the most in the league, and he adds 3 lost fumbles (51st). The picks are spread across short, intermediate and deep throws, so this isn't one bad read pattern; it's misplacement under any conditions. Some interception luck could even out, but a 4.8% rate over the last three games says the floor hasn't been found.

concerns.title: No vertical game without Pierce
concerns.body: Twelve percent completions on deep throws is part receiver and part passer. Pierce played two games before going to IR, and no one else on the roster is a vertical threat. But Jones's 2025 aDOT of 8.2 shows he can push the ball with the right weapon. Until Pierce returns, defenses can squeeze everything underneath.

trend.note: His only positive-EPA game came in Week 2 at Kansas City. Since Week 7 he has been at -0.318 EPA per dropback with a 5.3% interception rate, and the last two games (CPOE -18.6 and -16.3) were his worst accuracy performances of the year.

nextGame.headline: Weak Giants rush helps, but no tackles and no deep lane.
nextGame.body:
The Giants are a mid-pack defense (12th in EPA) with a specific shape. They barely pressure the quarterback (27th in hit rate, 24th in sack rate) but shut down deep passing (2nd in deep EPA allowed) and tight ends (TE1s run 3.0 PPR under their average, 3rd-best). That shape cuts both ways for Jones. The soft rush gives a struggling passer time. But time hasn't been his problem, and the throws that time enables, the deep ones, are exactly what New York takes away. Offenses also run a lot more than usual against them (pass rate 4.5 points under normal, 31st). That fits a Colts team whose run game is its best unit, and it points toward low pass volume as 6.5-point home underdogs with a 41.5 total.

Availability matters a great deal on the Colts' side. Both starting tackles, Jalen Travis (93% of snaps) and Bernhard Raimann (89%), are listed out. Against a weak rush that's survivable, but it's a real downgrade for a passer already missing throws from clean pockets. Pierce is still on IR, so there's no vertical answer. On the other side, starting corner Greg Newsome II (83% of snaps) is out for multiple weeks, which is the best news here for Downs and Allen working underneath and outside.

keyMatchups.title: Backup tackles vs a soft rush
keyMatchups.body: Losing both starting tackles would usually be a disaster. The Giants' pass rush, though, ranks near the bottom in both hits and sacks, which limits the damage. If the replacements hold up, Jones gets the cleanest pockets he has seen in weeks, and the game becomes a pure test of his accuracy.

keyMatchups.title: Downs and Allen without Newsome
keyMatchups.body: With a starting corner out, the Giants lose some of the coverage depth behind their good numbers against WR2s and WR3s. Jones's only reliable production comes from these two receivers. Feeding them on short and intermediate throws is the path to a functional day.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a top deep defense
keyMatchups.body: New York allows -0.281 EPA on deep throws, 2nd-best in the league, and Jones is completing 12.2% of his. Any forced vertical attempt is more likely to become a turnover than a big play.

nextGame.watch: His bad-throw rate on clean pockets: with the Giants unlikely to hit him much, misses here can't be blamed on the line.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect something close to the season line, not a return to 2025. The accuracy decline matches his early-career profile, the deep threat is on IR with only a slim chance of returning, and the line is banged up. Over the past five weeks he has averaged 136.8 passing yards a game on fewer attempts as Indianapolis leans on the run. That workload should continue, so 140-195 passing yards a game is a realistic band. Interceptions should ease a little from the current pace, because some of his picks reflect bad bounces as much as bad throws. But with this much inaccuracy, a rate near one a game is still the expectation. His touchdown rate, 2.0%, can't fall much further, so a modest bump is possible, especially near the goal line where he has six of his seven scores.

Rushing isn't going to rescue his floor. His carries are mostly sneaks, and his 2026 scrambles are fewer and less productive than in his Giants years. For fantasy purposes he is a low-end option whose value is capped by low volume and turnovers. For the Colts, his performance is the main reason a top-10 run game sits inside a 31st-ranked offense.
swingFactors: Travis and Raimann's return at tackle
Whether his bad-throw rate settles back toward 2025 levels

confidence.note: 11 starts is a solid sample and the career data supports the decline, but last season shows he has a higher ceiling in this system.
